name: Diego Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's mostly mechanical engineering, so statics, materials and a workshop session where we file a block of steel flat. Four days on campus, and Saturdays I stack shelves and cut keys at Harper's Hardware. I live in student housing, a corridor of eight, and I mostly keep to my room and the workshop. I don't use AI tools. I'd rather work it out by hand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you choose mechanical engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad has a machine shop with six people, Ito Precision, and I grew up sweeping the floor there. I liked seeing a drawing turn into a part you could hold. Mum does the books for it. They said I didn't have to join, but I think I want to know how things work before I decide anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything, and then people keep fixing the same pipes. I wouldn't say much online, since I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel a bit of relief, but my real worry is the shop. Dad's margins are thin, because a couple of big customers pay late. If things carry on as they are, it's tight but we manage. My degree is useful either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. Finish first-year modules, work Saturdays, and spend my holidays at the shop learning the machines. Maybe I'd show Dad how to use a simple quoting tool, if it saved him time, but I'd check it myself. I'm not going to hand over the numbers blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A bit uneasy, because the shop's money is a constant background worry, but that's not AI. It's just a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop's late payments are the real worry. What happens when a customer pays late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Late payments are the problem. One customer owes Dad about four months of invoices, and Mum chases them every week. If AI sped up that part, she'd be happy, but I think the money comes down to people deciding to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's behind your rule of not using AI for your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI because I want to know whether I understood something. If I paste a question in, I won't know if I've learned it. That's my rule, and it'd stay the same even if the tools got more useful.

say: I'd say it **sounds about right**: new things come along and people keep fixing the same pipes.
I wouldn't say much online, since I **don't really post**.
think: I'd feel **relief**, but my real worry is the **shop's thin margins**.
do: Finish **first-year modules** and keep Saturdays at the hardware store.
Spend holidays at **Dad's shop** learning the machines.
Try a simple **quoting tool** for Dad, checking it myself.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, because the shop's money is tight.
S0.quote: If I paste a question in, I won't know if I've learned it.
fieldNote: Diego's worry is the **family shop's late payments**, not AI itself.
His no-AI rule is about **knowing he understood**, a practical reason and not an ideology.
His tone is **laconic**, and he keeps feelings low-key.

steps.text: Work Saturdays at Harper's Hardware to cover costs
Test a simple quoting tool at Dad's shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we'll see. People said the same about computers in offices, and some jobs went, some came. I'd tell my mates on the course that a degree in making things is a decent place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think Mum's job is the exposed one. She does invoices, the books and chasing payments, and that's all screen work. If software does most of it, Dad might not need her full-time. That'd be a real hit at home, because her pay is part of what funds my course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to nudge Dad into trying the new tools, even though I don't like them either. I'd make sure the shop stays quick on quotes. And in my own studies I'd go towards design and workshop skills, the hands-on side, so I'm not in the group that gets squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not about me so much. It's about the shop and Mum. I don't like watching someone I know get told to change how she's worked for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum's job is the exposed one. What would change for her first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop has a CNC mill, and the programming of it is thinking work. If a program can write the machine code from a drawing, then one person could do what two do now. I'd want to be the person who understands the machine, not the one who types the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mum first, quietly. I'd ask what she'd want to learn if she had a choice. She's good with people and customers, and maybe the part of the job that's phone calls will stay human.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, because computers in offices didn't end work either.
I'd tell mates a degree in **making things** is a decent place to be.
think: **Mum's** job of invoices and books is the one that's **exposed**.
If software does it, Dad **might not need her** full-time, and her pay helps fund my course.
do: Nudge Dad to try **new quoting tools** so the shop stays fast.
Lean towards **design and workshop skills** in my studies.
Talk to **Mum** first about what she'd want to learn.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly about the shop and Mum, not about myself.
S1.quote: I'd want to be the person who understands the machine, not the one who types the code.
fieldNote: Diego's concern is **Mum's bookkeeping**, which is screen work and exposed, rather than his own studies.
He is reluctant about the tools but accepts they may be needed for the shop.
He proposes to talk **quietly** with his mum first, a sign of his private style.

steps.text: Show Dad a quoting tool during the winter break
Ask Mum what parts of her job she'd keep
Take the machine design and workshop modules
Ask my tutor which firms still hire apprentices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, slow down. Two years isn't enough for any business, school or family to make decent plans. I'd say it at home, and probably argue with my cousin, who thinks everything gets sorted out in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried. Mum's work would go first, then probably Dad's quoting and scheduling. I'd be at the end of my second year when the thinking side of engineering gets automated. I'd be thinking I might have put my time and my parents' money into the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course, because there's no better use of the time, and spend every free day at Dad's shop. If the shop is going to survive, it needs somebody who can run the machines and the software. I'd also cut costs, like selling my laptop's upgrade and cooking more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a heavy feeling, not a panicky one. I want to fix things but I don't know where to start, and that's frustrating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dad's customers might go quiet. How would you see that coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part I'd watch is whether the big customers start using automated suppliers. If a program can find the cheapest shop in seconds, Dad's loyal customers might go quiet. A small shop doesn't die in one day. It dies when the customers who always called us stop calling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dad I'll help, but he shouldn't take on any new debt for a machine right now. He loves buying a new machine when he's worried, so I'd have to say it plainly. It's the kind of thing I'd say once and then leave.

say: I'd say **slow down**: two years isn't enough for any family or firm to plan.
I'd argue with my cousin, who thinks it **gets sorted out**.
think: Mum's work would go first, then **Dad's quoting and scheduling**.
I might have put my **parents' money** into the wrong thing.
do: Stay on the course and spend free days at **Dad's shop**.
Learn to run both the **machines and the software**.
**Cook more** and skip upgrades to cut costs.
feel: **Anxious**, a heavy feeling rather than a panicky one.
S2.quote: A small shop doesn't die in one day. It dies when the customers who always called us stop calling.
fieldNote: Diego's picture of a **small shop slowly dying** is concrete and rooted in his dad's business.
He plans to hold steady and work in the shop, which suits his resistant style.
He worries about his dad **buying machines when frightened**, a family pattern he names.

steps.text: Work in Dad's shop every free weekend
Cook at home and skip the upgrade I wanted
Tell Dad not to take on machine debt
Ask the university hardship fund about support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, that gives a few years to see it. I'd tell people not to panic, but not to ignore it either. It's a bit like a flood forecast. You move the furniture upstairs, and you don't go on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried but steadier. I'd finish my degree in 2029, so I'd have about two years working, and Dad would have maybe five good years before he wants to slow down. The shop's timing is tight, and that's the real issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and go straight into a workshop or a plant, not a design office. I'd save for the shop, in case Dad wants to hand it over or close it. And I'd quietly learn how the new tools work, since I'd have to for the family's sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared, but heavy. There's a lot to carry, and I'd have to carry it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop's timing is the real issue. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Dad wants to retire or sell, I'd need to know the shop's numbers by then. I'd ask Mum to show me the books over the holidays. It's awkward, but I'd rather know the shop's real numbers than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your mum to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my plan is more about people than machines. A shop with six good people and loyal customers is worth something even if the machines change. I'd try to keep that part, and see whether the customers would stay.

say: I'd say it's like a **flood forecast**: move the furniture upstairs, but don't go on the news.
I'd tell people **not to panic**, and not to ignore it.
think: I'd have **two working years** after graduating, and Dad maybe five good years.
The **shop's timing** is tight, and that's the real issue.
do: Finish the degree and go straight into a **workshop or plant**.
**Save** in case Dad wants to hand over or close the shop.
Quietly **learn the new tools** for the family's sake.
feel: **Anxious**, not scared but heavy, with a lot to carry.
S3.quote: I'd rather know the shop's real numbers than guess.
fieldNote: Diego's flood image shows **quiet preparation** instead of public alarm.
He treats the shop's finances as his responsibility, which marks his **family loyalty**.
He is willing to learn the tools reluctantly, because it matters for the family.

steps.text: Save part of every Saturday wage for the shop
Apply to workshops and plants, not design offices
Ask Mum to show me the shop's books
Learn the machine-programming software on my own

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, a decade is long. A lot can happen, and a lot of it won't be what the headlines say. I'd tell friends to learn something real and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd feel almost normal. Ten years is long enough for me to finish, work, and understand the machines properly. I'd still worry about Dad, who'd be near retirement, but that could be handled. It doesn't scare me like the fast ones do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my degree, get a few years in a workshop, then see if the shop is a good place for me. I'd keep saving. And I'd probably end up using AI tools by then because everyone would, but I'd take my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, in the way it is when you know something's coming but not when. It doesn't take over my days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it be like to tell Dad's six people the shop is changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I took over the shop, it would be with fewer people and more machines. I'd be the one telling a few of them it's changing. I don't like that thought, because those six people have worked with Dad for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a natural with money. How would you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also learn the business side, because I think that's where I'd make mistakes. Mum could teach me some, and I'd take a short course. I'm not a natural with money, to be honest.

say: I'd say **a decade is long**, and a lot will not be what the headlines say.
I'd tell friends to **learn something real** and get on with it.
think: It'd feel **almost normal**, long enough to finish, work and understand the machines.
I'd still worry about **Dad** being near retirement, but it could be handled.
do: Finish the degree and spend a few years in a **workshop**.
Keep **saving** and decide about the shop later.
Use AI tools only when **everyone does**, and slowly.
feel: **Uneasy** a little, knowing something is coming but not when.
S4.quote: If I took over the shop, it would be with fewer people and more machines.
fieldNote: The long timeline brings Diego **calm**, though a sense of duty to the shop's six workers remains.
He admits he is **not good with money** and plans to learn from Mum.
He is willing to adopt AI later, once it's normal, which fits his resistant style.

steps.text: Save a deposit fund to take over the shop
Learn the shop's books from Mum each holiday
Take a short small-business finance course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because the shop has no room to move. Two years means Dad can't plan, and Mum's job goes early. What would help is some warning from the government and cheap loans so that a small shop can change slowly instead of closing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against new things. I just like to see them work before I trust them. People like me aren't stubborn for the sake of it, we just don't want to be the test case.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things. I just like to see them work before I trust them.
portrait: Diego is an **18-year-old** mechanical engineering student who works Saturdays at a hardware store.
His dad runs a six-person **machine shop** and his mum keeps the books, which makes his family's money tight.
He is centre-minded and **resistant** to new tech, and he does not use AI so he can know what he learned.
His fear is about the **shop and Mum's job**, not about his own degree.
He plans quietly, saves for the shop and would learn tools **only when needed**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries him most, because the shop has no room to move.
whatWouldHelp: **Early warning** and cheap loans so a small shop can change slowly instead of closing.
